Between AWS's June 30 and July 17 EC2 catalogs, the published on-demand price of the eight-GPU `p6-b300.48xlarge` in the Atlanta Local Zone fell from $167.3388 to $142.416 per hour for Linux, a 14.9% reduction. The equivalent SUSE, Ubuntu Pro, RHEL, and RHEL HA listings reflect the same underlying reduction. This is a verified price change for one instance family and location, not evidence of broader AWS or market-wide repricing.

Vultr had three region-specific listings that were no longer visible. This is a regional catalog reshuffle, not evidence of new capacity or retired hardware.

results.title: AI Inference Demand Just Surged 149% — and the GPU Market Is Tightening
highlights:
The Compute Tightness Index (CTI) tracks how tight GPU rental capacity is by comparing spot prices to on-demand prices and counting unavailable listings. A score above 60 means the market is tight. Above 80 is acute.

Compute Tightness Index — H200 Already Tight, Blended Still Balanced

The blended CTI sits at 47.5, still in the Balanced zone. But the aggregate masks what is happening at the GPU level. H200 is already tight at 66.6, up 10.9 points in the last 30 days. Its spot discount is only 25% compared to 56% for the older H100, which means spot buyers are paying close to on-demand prices for H200. B200 is balanced at 51.6. H100 is loose at 38.7, with 146 on-demand listings acting as a release valve.

The spot pricing confirms the tiering.

GPU Spot Rental Prices (Jul 20, 2026)

H100 is the bargain bin at $1.67 per hour on spot. H200 spot at $3.19 is nearly double. B200 commands $3.69 on spot, but the on-demand spread is massive at $7.18, reflecting the premium for Blackwell architecture. AMD's MI300X sits at $1.65 spot, competitive with H100 on price but with far fewer listings (3 spot vs 39 for H100).

results.title: GPU Compute Is Tightening at the High End
highlights:
The AI compute market is tightening at the high end. GPU spot rental prices rose 6.3% week over week for the H100/H200/B200 blend, driven almost entirely by H200 and B200 demand. H200 is now in "Tight" regime with a Compute Tightness Index of 66.6, while H100 remains loose and cheap. The bigger story is token demand: it jumped 38% in a single week to 58.5 trillion tokens, confirming that cheaper inference is pulling more GPU capacity into the market.

## The GPU market is splitting in two

Not all GPUs are tightening. The market is bifurcating between high-end cards that are scarce and older cards that still have slack.

| GPU | Spot Price (Jul 20) | WoW Change | CTI | Regime | On-Demand Unavailable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H200 | $3.19/hr | +7.4% | 66.6 | Tight | 32 of 60 |
| B200 | $3.69/hr | +7.3% | 51.6 | Balanced | 42 of 38 |
| H100 | $1.67/hr | +2.5% | 38.7 | Loose | 30 of 146 |

H200 is the bottleneck. More than half of on-demand listings are unavailable, and its CTI has risen 10.9 points in 30 days, the fastest tightening of any GPU in the index. B200 is following the same path: spot at $3.69 is still a 49% discount to on-demand pricing at $7.18, but availability is already strained. H100 is the relief valve: 146 on-demand listings, only 30 unavailable, and spot at $1.67, a 56% discount to on-demand. If H200 and B200 keep tightening, demand will spill into H100 and its price should catch up.

results.title: Bernstein: The Computing Power Market is Increasingly Displaying Commodity Characteristics (In-depth Report) | Bitget News
highlights:
Step one: Define a unified unit of measurement for computing power. The report points out that the biggest problem in today's computing power market is the "lack of comparability in raw computing power prices"—even for the same AI chip, there can be significant price differences between renting from a traditional hyperscaler cloud service provider and from a specialized neocloud provider. Index providers need to clearly define measurement units, such as using "NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB (including server, memory, bandwidth, etc.)" as the base unit and further refining standardization across layers (neocloud/hyperscaler), lease type (on-demand/committed term), region, and configuration.

...

Kalshi, a prediction market platform regulated by the CFTC, has launched prediction contracts tied to GPU rental prices, and on July 14, it rolled out computing power price curves for the B200, H200, and A100 chips—B200 was quoted at $5.41, with a historical peak of $7.39.

results.title: AI Tokenomics Depends on Memory, Not Just GPUs | WEKA
highlights:
Evan: So the price of an on-demand GPU — one where you have a guarantee that you will get that on-demand node — can be $10 an hour, or upwards of $10 an hour. And the price of that same GPU sold as preemptible, sold as “you’re not sure if you’re going to get it,” can be 50 cents. So I would say that the majority of the cost of a GPU hour is risk. Beyond that, there’s all sorts of other things we can optimize toward, but mostly it’s risk.

...

Carmen: So, I definitely echo that. It depends on the commercial contract — the cost can be very different regionally, and different GPUs, even the same H100 family or B200 family, can cost differently depending on the CPU, the RAM, and other spec differences. Right now, hyperscalers obviously charge a premium over the clouds overall — probably 2x to 3x on-demand instances around the world. But we see GPU costs not only being high, but also volatile. High is one thing — if it doesn’t move, I guess that can actually be a good thing, since you know what you’re going to pay the next hour. The problem is it moves all the time.

...
